title: Krishna's Counsel: Peace Before War
subtitle: Duty is weighed against the cost of conflict

learningObjectives.text: What does the poem say Yudhishthira prizes above empire?
What does Krishna ask Dhrita-rashtra to do?

duty.author: traditionally attributed to Vyasa
duty.locator: Book VII · UDYOGA; Book VII · UDYOGA, normalized characters 1850-2481
duty.excerpt: Known to all, ye mighty monarchs! May your glory ever last! True to plighted word Yudhishthir hath his weary exile passed, Twelve long years with fair Draupadi in the pathless jungle strayed, And a year in menial service in Virata's palace stayed, He hath kept his plighted promise, braved affliction, woe and shame, And he begs, assembled monarchs, ye shall now his duty name! For he swerveth not from duty kingdom of the sky to win, Prizeth hamlet more than empire, so his course be free from sin, Loss of realm and wealth and glory higher virtues in him prove, Thoughts of peace and not of anger still the good Yudhishthir move!
duty.note: Verbatim English translation from Dutt. The Mahabharata volume is a condensed verse rendering; the Ramayana volume contains only the Balakandam and Ayodhyakandam.

counsel.author: traditionally attributed to Vyasa
counsel.locator: Book VII · UDYOGA; Book VII · UDYOGA, normalized characters 10208-10915
counsel.excerpt: Seek not war and death of kinsmen, word of peace and love I bring! 'Midst the wide earth's many nations Bharats in their worth excel, Love and kindness, spotless virtue, in the Kuru-elders dwell, Father of the noble nation, now retired from life's turmoil, Ill beseems that sin or untruth should thy ancient bosom soil! For thy sons in impious anger seek to do their kinsmen wrong, And withhold the throne and kingdom which by right to them belong, And a danger thus ariseth like the comet's baleful fire, Slaughtered kinsmen, bleeding nations, soon shall feed its fatal ire! Stretch thy hands, O Kuru monarch! prove thy truth and holy grace, Man of peace! avert the slaughter and preserve thy ancient race.
counsel.note: Verbatim English translation from Dutt. The Mahabharata volume is a condensed verse rendering; the Ramayana volume contains only the Balakandam and Ayodhyakandam.

narrativeBlocks.title: A kingdom is disputed
narrativeBlocks.body: In Dutt's condensed verse rendering of the Mahabharata, Krishna addresses a council while the Pandavas seek the return of their kingdom after exile.

narrativeBlocks.title: Krishna asks for counsel
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Dutt's English rendering; whitespace normalized): “Seek not war and death of kinsmen, word of peace and love I bring! 'Midst the wide earth's many nations Bharats in their worth excel, Love and kindness, spotless virtue, in the Kuru-elders dwell, Father of the noble nation, now retired from life's turmoil, Ill beseems that sin or untruth should thy ancient bosom soil! For thy sons in impious anger seek to do their kinsmen wrong, And withhold the throne and kingdom which by right to them belong, And a danger thus ariseth like the comet's baleful fire, Slaughtered kinsmen, bleeding nations, soon shall feed its fatal ire! Stretch thy hands, O Kuru monarch! prove thy truth and holy grace, Man of peace! avert the slaughter and preserve thy ancient race.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A claim without eager war
narrativeBlocks.body: Krishna describes Yudhishthira as preferring even a small settlement to empire if it can be gained without sin, and asks the assembled rulers how to proceed.

narrativeBlocks.title: Do not turn one epic scene into a universal rule
narrativeBlocks.body: This is Romesh Chunder Dutt's nineteenth-century condensed verse rendering. It gives one literary portrayal of deliberation, not a complete account of dharma across Indian traditions.

narrativeBlocks.title: The choice is political and ethical
narrativeBlocks.body: The council scene connects a disputed inheritance with questions about peace, justice, and the cost of war.
